newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, congressional leaders talk cooperation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, congressional leaders talk cooperation.

text.p: In a U.S. capital radiating conciliatory political talk, President Bill Clinton and congressional Republicans agreed on Tuesday on a handful of goals including a balanced federal budget by 2002.

Flanked by Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich, both Republicans, the Democratic president told reporters this rare bipartisan meeting was "a very important first step" toward progress on the budget, education and other issues.
"It is an indication we want to work together," Clinton said of the meeting in the President's Room just off the Senate floor.

"I think it is imperative that we pass a bipartisan balanced budget this year. And, I think it is imperative that we find a way to work together on education reform. We'll be talking about how we can do that and many other things."

Lott and Gingrich, who had tangled with Clinton over the budget in the past two years, later called the meeting very positive and said they had agreed to work on five or six specific goals in the context of a balanced budget by 2002.

While there were clearly areas of disagreement such as campaign finance reform, the Republicans said there was a new atmosphere of conciliation. "We're trying to find a way to take the minimum number of potshots at each other and get on with our work," Lott said.

Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, listed the areas on they had agreed to work as: efforts to move people from welfare rolls into jobs, a review of Clinton's education reform proposals, improving juvenile justice, helping the financially floundering city of Washington, and meetings between Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and the chairmen of congressional tax-writing committees to seek agreement on tax cuts.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, said he wanted to add health care for children but Republicans were not ready to add this goal.

"Rather than come together and argue over the things we disagree on we thought that (it would be) an opportunity to begin to identify issues where we can work together," Lott of Mississippi said at the outset of the meeting.
Other leaders from both parties, including House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, also attended as did Vice President Al Gore and Rubin.

The invitation to the president represented a sea change for Republicans. Last year they tried to force the White House to accept their conservative agenda and then found the public blamed them, not Clinton, for the government shutdowns.
Clinton last week presented his new budget, winning a cool reception from Republicans.

The president's proposal envisions the government's budget being brought into balance by 2002 and remaining there for the next 10 to 20 years, a sharp contrast with the past 26 years of rising red ink in Washington.

To get there, some of the headway made against the deficit in the last four years would be lost. Clinton's plan would not produce a deficit below 1996's $107 billion until the year 2000. It would add spending for education and welfare and give families a $98 billion tax cut over the five years. And it would raise other taxes by $76 billion and reduce Medicare.

Whether Republicans come up with a separate attempt to balance the budget by the year 2002 remains to be decided. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said they will decide after they have seen how much progress is made in the budget committees.

But Republicans said Clinton's plan would be the starting point for talks on spending and taxes. Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said it was "alive on arrival," unlike last year's plan, which was trashed before entering the Capitol doors.
